triage.name: Epididymitis
triage.reason: Acute scrotal pain with gradual onset and urinary symptoms; key differential with testicular torsion, worked up by history, exam, urinalysis and ultrasound.

demographics: Most common cause of acute scrotal pain in postpubertal males
Sexually active young men are affected most often
Older men with urinary obstruction or recent instrumentation are also affected

risk_factors.text: Sexually transmitted infection such as chlamydia or gonorrhea
Recent urinary tract instrumentation or catheterization
Urinary tract obstruction or benign prostatic hyperplasia

chief_complaints.text: The pain came on slowly over a day or two
One side of my scrotum is swollen

hpi.duration: Usually present for a few days at presentation
hpi.progression: Pain and swelling build up gradually and may spread from the epididymis to the whole testicle and scrotum
hpi.location: Unilateral, usually starting in the epididymis at the back of the testicle
hpi.radiation: May radiate along the spermatic cord to the groin or lower abdomen
pertinent_negatives: Pain that woke me from sleep

argues_against: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
Nausea and vomiting preceding scrotal pain

atypical.how_it_differs: Epididymitis is uncommon before puberty; when it occurs, it often follows a urinary tract infection or an anatomic abnormality, and the child may only be irritable or refuse to walk.
More often associated with benign prostatic hyperplasia, catheterization or urinary tract infection, and symptoms may be milder with less fever.
Can be caused by unusual organisms and may progress to abscess or necrosis with fewer local signs.

general.mild: Comfortable at rest, mild scrotal discomfort, no systemic illness
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, prefers to lie still, may limp or walk slowly
general.severe: Ill-appearing, febrile, guarding the scrotum, reluctant to move
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, diaphoretic, severe pain, possible scrotal necrosis or sepsis

findings.maneuver: Palpate the scrotal contents, starting with the unaffected side, then gently palpate the epididymis on the affected side
findings.finding: Tenderness localized to the epididymis, especially the tail
Redness of the scrotal skin on the affected side

findings.maneuver: Elevate the scrotum manually or ask the patient to lie down with scrotal support
findings.finding: Relief of scrotal pain with elevation

findings.maneuver: Palpate the spermatic cord from the external inguinal ring to the testis
Palpate the testis itself after examining the epididymis
findings.finding: Testis is non-tender and normal in consistency

findings.maneuver: Stroke the inner thigh and observe for testicular elevation
Shine a light through the scrotum in a darkened room
findings.finding: No transillumination of the scrotal swelling

findings.maneuver: Palpate the testis for any discrete mass
Inspect the urethral meatus and milk the urethra if discharge is suspected

labs.caveat: Pyuria supports an infectious cause but is nonspecific; it can be absent early or in noninfectious epididymitis.
Positive nitrite points to a gram-negative urinary pathogen and is more typical of older men with obstruction than of sexually transmitted infection.
A normal white count does not exclude epididymitis.
Not applicable in males; listed only to note it is never part of this workup.

imaging.preferred_when: All patients with acute scrotal pain where torsion is a concern; first-line imaging

findings.text: Increased blood flow in the epididymis on color Doppler
Thickened scrotal skin and soft tissue edema
Normal or increased testicular blood flow (helps exclude torsion)
Normal testis without a discrete mass
Scrotal abscess or testicular infarction (complicated disease)

imaging.preferred_when: When Doppler ultrasound is unavailable or nondiagnostic and torsion must be excluded

findings.text: Increased radiotracer uptake in the affected epididymis and testis (increased perfusion)
Normal or increased testicular perfusion, arguing against torsion

imaging.preferred_when: Rarely needed; when ultrasound is equivocal and torsion or abscess is still suspected

findings.text: Enhancing, enlarged epididymis with surrounding inflammatory change

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

findings.text: Not used for scrotal pain; may incidentally show an enlarged epididymis or hydrocele when performed for other reasons

initial.why: Pyuria, bacteriuria and nitrite support a urinary source; also screens for hematuria and stones
Leukocytosis with left shift supports infection and gauges severity
Confirms epididymitis and, most importantly, excludes testicular torsion
initial.only_if: torsion cannot be confidently excluded by history and exam, or the diagnosis is uncertain

supporting.why: Supports an inflammatory or infectious process when the diagnosis is unclear
Nonspecific marker of inflammation; occasionally helpful
Alternative when Doppler ultrasound is unavailable or nondiagnostic
supporting.only_if: ultrasound is equivocal and torsion remains a concern

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: No role in scrotal pain; exposes the patient to radiation without adding diagnostic value
Reserved for rare equivocal cases; not part of routine workup
Not needed unless pain is epigastric

decision_points: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency: if sudden severe pain, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex or abnormal lie is present, do not delay for imaging — urology/surgery immediately
Ultrasound with color Doppler is the first-line study when torsion cannot be excluded clinically
In sexually active young men, treat empirically for chlamydia and gonorrhea and test for STIs; in older men or those with instrumentation, cover enteric organisms
Consider abscess or infarction if fever and pain worsen despite appropriate antibiotics

differential.name: Testicular torsion
differential.why_considered: Acute unilateral scrotal pain in a young male is torsion until proven otherwise
differential.trigger: Sudden severe pain, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex, or abnormal testicular lie

history: Abrupt onset, often waking the patient from sleep
exam: High-riding, transversely lying testis
Absent cremasteric reflex
Diffuse testicular tenderness rather than epididymal localization
No relief with scrotal elevation
imaging: Reduced or absent testicular blood flow on color Doppler ultrasound
Whirlpool sign of the spermatic cord
Radionuclide scan shows a cold testis

differential.name: Orchitis
differential.why_considered: Unilateral scrotal pain and swelling with fever, often viral in origin

exam: Tenderness and enlargement of the testis itself rather than the epididymis
Testis may be firm and swollen
labs: Mumps serology or viral testing when suspected
imaging: Enlarged, heterogeneous testis with increased or heterogeneous Doppler flow

differential.name: Testicular cancer
differential.why_considered: Painless or mildly painful testicular enlargement in a young man
differential.trigger: Firm, painless testicular mass or unexplained testicular enlargement

exam: Discrete firm testicular mass
Testis not diffusely tender
Possible supraclavicular or abdominal mass from metastases

differential.name: Torsion of the appendix testis
differential.why_considered: Focal scrotal pain in a younger male with a tender nodule

exam: Tender nodule at the upper pole of the testis
Blue dot sign on transillumination
Normal testis and epididymis otherwise
imaging: Normal testicular and epididymal Doppler flow
Small avascular nodule at the upper pole

differential.name: Inguinal hernia
differential.why_considered: Groin and scrotal swelling with discomfort

history: Swelling worse with standing, straining or coughing
exam: Palpable inguinal or scrotal bulge that may reduce
Bowel sounds in the scrotum if containing bowel
Tenderness over the cord rather than the epididymis
imaging: Ultrasound shows bowel or omentum in the inguinal canal or scrotum

differential.name: Varicocele
differential.why_considered: Scrotal heaviness and swelling, usually on the left

history: Dull ache worse with standing and at the end of the day
exam: Bag of worms texture above the testis
Worse with Valsalva
Left side predominance
imaging: Dilated veins greater than 2–3 mm on ultrasound with reversal of flow on Valsalva

differential.name: Hydrocele
differential.why_considered: Painless or mildly uncomfortable scrotal swelling

exam: Fluid collection that transilluminates
Testis and epididymis palpable and non-tender
imaging: Anechoic fluid around the testis on ultrasound

differential.name: Fournier gangrene
differential.why_considered: Severe scrotal pain and swelling with systemic toxicity, especially in diabetes
differential.trigger: Pain out of proportion to findings, crepitus, skin necrosis or rapid progression in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient

history: Systemic illness with fever and malaise
exam: Crepitus in the scrotal or perineal skin
Dusky or necrotic skin
Pain out of proportion to examination
Tachycardia and hypotension
imaging: CT showing gas in the soft tissues and fascial planes
Ultrasound may show subcutaneous gas and fluid

severity.mild: Gradual onset over 1–2 days, mild scrotal discomfort, no fever, urinalysis with trace leukocyte esterase, able to walk comfortably
severity.moderate: Established infection with moderate pain, unilateral swelling and erythema, low-grade fever, pyuria and leukocytosis, prefers to lie still
severity.severe: Marked pain and swelling, high fever and chills, systemic illness, significant leukocytosis, possible early abscess
severity.critical: Complicated disease with scrotal abscess, testicular infarction, Fournier gangrene or sepsis with hypotension and organ dysfunction

red_flags.finding: Sudden severe pain with high-riding testis or absent cremasteric reflex
red_flags.meaning: Testicular torsion until proven otherwise; needs immediate urologic evaluation and surgery

red_flags.finding: Pain out of proportion to examination with crepitus or dusky skin
red_flags.meaning: Fournier gangrene; surgical emergency requiring debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics
Sepsis; needs resuscitation and urgent source control

red_flags.finding: Fluctuant scrotal mass or worsening pain despite antibiotics
red_flags.meaning: Scrotal abscess or testicular infarction; requires imaging and possible drainage

red_flags.finding: Testicular mass or unexplained firm enlargement
red_flags.meaning: Testicular cancer must be excluded with ultrasound and tumor markers

complications.name: Testicular infarction
clues: Absent or markedly reduced testicular Doppler flow

complications.name: Fournier gangrene
clues: Pain out of proportion to findings

complications.name: Chronic epididymitis and chronic scrotal pain
clues: Pain persisting more than 6 weeks after treatment

complications.name: Epididymal obstruction and subfertility
clues: Infertility evaluation showing obstructive azoospermia or oligospermia

special_populations.differences: Epididymitis is uncommon before puberty; consider anatomic abnormalities or urinary tract infection. Torsion is more likely and must be excluded urgently. The child may only be irritable or refuse to walk.
More often associated with benign prostatic hyperplasia, catheterization or urinary tract infection; enteric organisms are more likely. Symptoms may be milder with less fever.
Higher risk of severe infection, abscess and Fournier gangrene; maintain a lower threshold for imaging and aggressive treatment.
Can be caused by unusual organisms and may progress to abscess or necrosis with fewer local signs; consider broader antimicrobial coverage.

key_questions.question: How did the pain start — suddenly or gradually over hours to days?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over 1–2 days; sudden severe onset suggests testicular torsion

key_questions.question: Where exactly is the pain, and does it radiate?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral pain localized to the back of the testicle, radiating along the spermatic cord to the groin or lower abdomen

key_questions.question: Does the pain get better when you lift or support the scrotum?
key_questions.looking_for: Relief with scrotal elevation (Prehn sign) supports epididymitis over torsion

key_questions.question: Does it burn or hurt when you urinate? Are you going more often or urgently?
key_questions.looking_for: Dysuria, frequency or urgency suggesting a urinary tract source

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any discharge from the penis?
key_questions.looking_for: Urethral discharge suggesting chlamydia or gonorrhea

key_questions.question: Have you had fever or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever and chills suggesting systemic infection; high fever with toxicity raises concern for abscess or Fournier gangrene

key_questions.question: Are you sexually active? Do you have a new partner or more than one partner? Do you use condoms?
key_questions.looking_for: STI risk factors that guide empiric coverage for chlamydia and gonorrhea

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent urinary catheter, cystoscopy or urologic procedure?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent instrumentation suggesting enteric organisms and a different antibiotic choice

key_questions.question: Do you have trouble urinating, a weak stream, or a history of prostate problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Benign prostatic hyperplasia or obstruction, more typical in older men

key_questions.question: Have you ever had this pain before, or any testicular trauma?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior similar episodes or trauma; trauma raises concern for hematoma or rupture

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes or any condition that weakens your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes or immunosuppression, which raises the risk of severe infection such as Fournier gangrene

key_questions.question: Are you taking any medications, especially amiodarone?
key_questions.looking_for: Amiodarone is a recognized cause of epididymitis

key_questions.question: Have you had nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Nausea and vomiting at onset suggest torsion rather than epididymitis

key_questions.question: Have you noticed a lump in the testicle or blood in the urine?
key_questions.looking_for: A painless firm testicular mass suggests cancer; hematuria suggests stones or another urinary source

reasoning_points: Gradual onset of unilateral scrotal pain over 1–2 days rather than sudden severe pain
Pain localized to the epididymis, often with tenderness along the spermatic cord and relief with scrotal elevation
Associated urinary symptoms such as dysuria, frequency or urgency, and sometimes urethral discharge
Risk factors identified: sexually transmitted infection in a young man, or obstruction, catheterization or instrumentation in an older man
Fever and leukocytosis may be present but are not required
Urinalysis showing pyuria and possibly bacteriuria supports a urinary source
Scrotal ultrasound with color Doppler confirms an enlarged, hyperemic epididymis and, most importantly, excludes testicular torsion
Testicular torsion must be considered and excluded first because it is a surgical emergency

easy: Sexually active young man with gradual unilateral scrotal pain, dysuria and urethral discharge
Tenderness localized to the epididymis with relief on scrotal elevation
Ultrasound shows an enlarged, hyperemic epididymis with normal testicular flow
medium: Older man with benign prostatic hyperplasia or recent catheterization and milder symptoms
Mild pyuria with a normal white count
Overlap with orchitis or a reactive hydrocele on exam
Need to distinguish from torsion of the appendix testis in a younger patient
hard: Early presentation with minimal swelling and no urinary symptoms
Diabetic or immunocompromised patient with severe pain out of proportion to findings suggesting Fournier gangrene
Persistent fever and worsening pain despite antibiotics suggesting scrotal abscess or infarction
Painless firm testicular enlargement that turns out to be cancer rather than epididymitis
Prepubertal boy who is irritable and refuses to walk, where torsion must be excluded urgently
